system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2131-06-02 15:15:00 to 2131-06-04 15:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and multiple abdominal surgeries was admitted for acute on chronic abdominal pain. The pain was consistent with a flare of chronic pancreatitis, without evidence of obstruction on CT imaging. He was managed supportively with NPO status, IV fluids, and IV pain control, then advanced to a regular diet as symptoms improved. His blood sugars were low due to poor oral intake, prompting temporary discontinuation of insulin and metformin. Pain and mood improved during the stay. He was discharged home with oral pain medication, Miralax, continued pancreatic enzymes, and instructions to restart diabetes medications when eating normally and blood sugars exceed 130, along with follow-up in outpatient care.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST RADIOGRAPHS

HISTORY:  Chest pain and cough.

COMPARISONS:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Chest, PA and lateral.

FINDINGS:  The heart is normal in size.  The mediastinal and hilar contours
appear within normal limits.  The lungs appear clear.  There are no pleural
effusions or pneumothorax.  Bony structures are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of acute disease.

CTA OF THE CHEST

HISTORY:  Severe chest and abdominal pain with shortness of breath,
tachycardia and abdominal tenderness.  Prior history of pulmonary emboli, now
off of Coumadin; also history of small bowel obstruction.

COMPARISONS:  A CT of the abdomen is available from ___ and a CT
of the chest is available from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Following a non-contrast CT of the chest, multidetector CT images
of the chest were obtained with intravenous contrast in the pulmonary arterial
phase.  Sagittal and coronal reformations were also performed.

FINDINGS:  

CT TORSO: Coronary artery calcifications are present.  The heart is normal in
size.  Trace pericardial fluid appears within normal limits.  There are no
pleural effusions.  No enlarged lymph nodes are demonstrated.  There are no
filling defects among the pulmonary arteries.

A small focus of bronchiectasis in the left lower lobe where peripheral
bronchiole is dilated to 2 mm (2:26), which is not significantly changed.  

CT ABDOMEN:  The patient is status post cholecystectomy.  The liver, adrenal
glands and spleen appear within normal limits.  Widespread pancreatic
calcifications are consistent with chronic pancreatitis.  A few small
hypoattenuating foci in the right kidney are too small to characterize but
unchanged.  There is slightly prominent fluid in distal small bowel but
without dilatation or wall thickening.  The post-surgical appearance of the
stomach, small and large bowel is unremarkable, noting prior Puestow surgery
with Roux-en-Y.  There is perhaps a very small umbilical hernia containing
fat, but no substantial ventral hernia.

CT PELVIS:  The prostate, seminal vesicles, and bladder appear within normal
limits.  Patchy vascular calcifications are present.  There is no aneurysm. 
The major mesenteric arteries and veins appear patent.  There is no ascites or
lymphadenopathy.  Small left-sided paraaortic lymph nodes are unchanged and do
not meet CT size criteria for pathological enlargement, although they are
mildly prominent by number but unchanged.

BONE WINDOWS:  Mild-to-moderate degenerative changes are present along the
lower lumbar facets.  There is mild leftward convex curvature centered along
the mid lumbar spine.  There are no suspicious lytic or blastic lesions.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence for pulmonary emboli or other acute process.

2.  Coronary artery calcifications.

3.  No evidence for bowel obstruction.

4.  Findings consistent with chronic pancreatitis, including widespread
pancreatic calcifications, with stable findings status post Puestow with
Roux-en-Y.

INDICATION:  ___ man with right-sided numbness and weakness, to
evaluate for intracranial pathology.

COMPARISON:  CT head without contrast, ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT imaging of the head was performed without
intravenous contrast.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, edema, masses, or
mass effect.  The gray-white matter differentiation is well preserved.  The
ventricles and sulci are mildly prominent, consistent with mild involutional
changes.  The basal cisterns are normal. Imaged paranasal sinuses and mastoid
air cells are clear.  The orbits are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intracranial pathology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this sharp pain in my upper belly for about four days now. It’s different from my usual pancreatitis pain. I’ve also been vomiting greenish stuff and haven’t had a bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned black stool recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one time. I was worried it might be blood. My gastroenterologist told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We ran some tests. Your blood work shows your white count is a bit high, which suggests inflammation, but your pancreas enzymes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It still could be a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. Sometimes the enzymes don’t rise. We also saw calcifications in your pancreas on the CT scan, which is consistent with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the black stool? Is there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your stool in the ER and it was guaiac positive, meaning there’s a small amount of blood. But the CT didn’t show any obvious source, and no signs of bowel obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve had so many surgeries, I was afraid something was blocked again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping an eye on it. You’re passing gas, which is a good sign. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and monitor your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugars have been really low too—like 30—without taking any meds. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely because you haven’t been eating much. Your body doesn’t have enough glucose stores. We’ve held your insulin and metformin for now, which is safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m supposed to be getting workup for hypoglycemia at the VA. Access is down, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make a note to follow up with them. For now, we’ll keep monitoring your sugars. They’re at 146 now, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I also noticed my right hand and foot feel numb. That’s new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned that. We did a CT of your head to rule out stroke, and it was normal. It might be related to nerve issues from diabetes or something else. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s making my walk a bit off too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll assess your strength and coordination daily. For now, we don’t see anything urgent on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but the medicine helps. I’m starving though. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on clear liquids tonight. If that goes well, you can try a light meal tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I already ordered a hamburger in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s stick to broth and tea for now. We don’t want to aggravate your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You tolerated the clear liquids well. We’re going to advance you to a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Any chance I can get that hamburger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Maybe later. Start with toast, applesauce, and maybe some grilled chicken. Small portions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. How’s my kidney? I remember you said it was stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was elevated when you came in—1.2, up from your baseline of 0.8. But it’s likely due to dehydration. With IV fluids, it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no permanent damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like a temporary, pre-renal issue. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look good. Pain is better, you’re eating, and your kidney function is recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll give you a few pain and nausea pills to take home, but use them sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know not to mix them with alcohol. I’ve learned that the hard way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, restart your diabetes meds when you’re eating regularly and your sugars are above 130.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the numbness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still mild, and no new changes. It may be chronic neuropathy. Mention it to your PCP for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your symptoms have improved with supportive care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll call my PCP like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep taking your pancreatic enzymes with meals, plus the omeprazole and Miralax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right path. Take it easy for a few days and call if the pain worsens or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and multiple abdominal surgeries was admitted for acute epigastric pain, nausea, and bilious vomiting lasting four days, along with a report of black stool. Initial evaluation revealed leukocytosis and guaiac-positive stool, but normal pancreatic enzymes and no evidence of bowel obstruction or pulmonary embolism on CT imaging. His acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal from dehydration, resolved with IV fluids. Pain improved with supportive care, and he was advanced to a regular diet. New right-sided numbness and weakness were noted but CT head showed no acute pathology. He was discharged home with improved symptoms, instructions to restart diabetes medications with adequate intake, and follow-up with his primary care provider.
